pr_md.text:
# Audit and fix: orders-service

Read-only audit of `src/` against `README.md`, then a fix for each defect that
reproduced. Six defects reproduced before the change and no longer reproduce
after it. The visible suite passed with all six present, so each fixed
behaviour gained a regression test.

## What changed

### Security

**1. Any customer could read any other customer's order** — `src/orders/routes.js`

`GET /orders/:id` called `orders.get(id)`, which does no ownership check, while
every sibling route used `orders.getOwned(user, id)`. Any authenticated
customer could read another customer's order — items, prices, total, and the
owner's user id — by guessing or obtaining its id. README: "Customers read and
change only their own orders and payments." Now uses `getOwned`, so a non-owner
gets 404, matching the README rule that an invisible resource is a 404.

**2. Report download could read any file on disk** — `src/reports/routes.js`

`GET /reports/:name` passed the path parameter straight into
`path.join(reportDir, params.name)`. The router URI-decodes path parameters, so
`GET /reports/..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd` escaped `REPORT_DIR` and returned the
file's contents to any admin. Export names are generated by this module, so the
fix is a whitelist on the generated shape (`/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.csv$/`): no path
separator, and no dot in the stem, so `..` cannot be formed. A rejected name
returns 404 rather than 400, because a name that cannot denote a report is
indistinguishable from a report that does not exist.

**3. Login response time revealed which emails are registered** — `src/users/service.js`

`verifyCredentials` returned early when no user matched, skipping the scrypt
hash. A registered email cost ~20 ms, an unknown one ~0.7 ms — a 28x difference,
measurable remotely, which turns the login endpoint into an account-enumeration
oracle. It now compares against a per-process dummy hash when no user matches,
so both paths perform exactly one scrypt and one `timingSafeEqual`.

### Correctness

**4. Order totals were not exact to the cent** — `src/lib/money.js`, `src/orders/service.js`

`sumLines` summed `unitPrice * quantity` in floating point, so an order for 3
items at 0.1 was stored and served with `total: 0.30000000000000004`. README:
"An order total is exact to the cent." Totals are now accumulated in integer
cents and converted once at the end.

**5. `totalPages` under-reported the number of pages** — `src/lib/pagination.js`

`Math.floor(items.length / pageSize)` instead of `Math.ceil`. With 24 orders at
`pageSize=10` the response said `totalPages: 2` while page 3 held 4 more items,
so a client paginating on `totalPages` silently dropped the last partial page.
Any item count below one page already reported 1 via the `Math.max(1, …)`
clamp, which is why no visible test caught it.

**6. Shipped orders could be cancelled** — `src/orders/service.js`

`TRANSITIONS.shipped` listed `cancelled`. README: "a shipped or delivered order
can no longer be cancelled." Removed; `shipped` now transitions only to
`delivered`.

### Dead code

- **`parseCookies`** (`src/http/respond.js`) — removed. No caller anywhere in
  `src/` or `test/`; the service authenticates by `Authorization` header only
  and reads no cookies.
- **`registerProvider`** (`src/payments/providers.js`) — removed. Exported but
  never called from outside the module, which called it once at load time to
  register the single `manual` provider. Its validation guarded a call site
  that does not exist. The provider table is now a module constant, and
  `getProvider` keeps the `provider: '<name>'` option and its unknown-name
  error unchanged. A `Map` rather than an object literal, so a name like
  `constructor` cannot resolve through the prototype chain.

`users.toPublic` is **not** in this category: it had a live caller before the
change. It left the service's public surface as a consequence of the layering
fix below, which removed the only call site.

### Simplification

**Order total had two implementations.** `src/payments/service.js` carried its
own `orderTotalCents`, correctly summing in cents, while `src/orders/service.js`
summed in floats. The two disagreed for the same order: payment validation
accepted the exact total while the API advertised the inexact one, so defect 4
could not be observed through the payment path. Cent arithmetic now lives in
`src/lib/money.js` (`toCents`, `fromCents`, `totalCents`) and the payment
service compares the submitted amount against `order.total`. The orders
subsystem owns the total; payments reads it.

**The user route reached past its service into the store.** `GET /users` built
its response from `store.list('users').map(users.toPublic)` inside
`src/users/routes.js` — the only reason the route layer received `store` at all,
and the only list endpoint that paginated in the route rather than the service
(`orders.list` paginates in the service). Replaced with `users.list(query)`;
`store` is no longer passed to `registerUserRoutes`, so the route layer now
depends only on services.

## Evidence

All commands run from the repository root on Node.js 20+, Windows.

**Baseline before any change** — `node --test`:

```
ℹ tests 20
ℹ pass 20
ℹ fail 0
```

**After the change** — `node --test`:

```
ℹ tests 25
ℹ pass 25
ℹ fail 0
```

**The five new tests fail against the original source.** Restoring `src/` from
`HEAD` and running the new suite (`git checkout HEAD -- src && node --test`):

```
✖ an order is hidden from customers who do not own it
✖ an order total is exact to the cent
✖ a shipped or delivered order can no longer be cancelled
✖ a page reports every page needed to show its items
✖ a report name cannot reach outside the report directory
ℹ tests 25
ℹ pass 20
ℹ fail 5
```

This check caught a hollow assertion: the first version of the cent-exactness
test used two line items (0.1x3 plus 0.2x1) whose float errors cancelled, so it
passed against the buggy code. It was rewritten around single line items
(0.1x3 to 0.3, 1.1x3 to 3.3), where the error is observable.

**End-to-end probe against a live server**, driving the real HTTP surface with
an admin and two customers, before and after. A file was planted next to
`REPORT_DIR` for the traversal probe:

| Probe | Before | After |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `GET /orders/:id` for another customer's order | `200` with the full order | `404 {"error":"order not found"}` |
| Order total for 0.1 x 3 | `0.30000000000000004` | `0.3` |
| `GET /orders?pageSize=10` over 24 orders | `totalPages: 2`, page 3 holds 4 items | `totalPages: 3` |
| `POST /orders/:id/cancel` on a shipped order | `200`, status `cancelled` | `409` |
| `GET /reports/..%2FSECRET-OUTSIDE.txt` | `200` with the outside file's contents | `404 {"error":"report not found"}` |
| `POST /sessions` latency, wrong password | known email 20.1 ms vs unknown 0.7 ms | 20.1 ms vs 20.1 ms |

**Unit-level checks** of the rewritten libraries (`node -e`):

```
0.1 x 3 -> 0.3
12.5x2 + 5x1 -> 30
24 items, pageSize 10 -> totalPages 3
0 items -> totalPages 1
2 items -> totalPages 1
```

**Dead-code claims** were established by walking every `module.exports` symbol
in `src/` and searching `src/` and `test/` for a caller outside its own file.
Before: two symbols had none — `http/respond.js -> parseCookies` and
`payments/providers.js -> registerProvider`. After: none.

**Measured structural effect.** The module import graph is *unchanged* by the
simplification: 17 modules, 25 internal import edges, longest import chain 3,
no cycles, before and after. The coupling removed from the user route was
injected at runtime rather than imported, so it does not appear in that
projection. What moved, measured:

| Projection | Before | After |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Collaborators injected into route modules | 11 | 10 |
| Route modules receiving the store | 1 | 0 |
| Implementations of order-total arithmetic | 2 | 1 |
| Exported symbols with no caller | 2 | 0 |
| Import cycles | none | none |

Total exported symbols stayed at 27: three removals (`parseCookies`,
`registerProvider`, `sumLines`) against three additions (`toCents`,
`fromCents`, `totalCents`) plus `users.list` for `users.toPublic`. This change
consolidates duplicated arithmetic and a layering violation; it does not make
the module graph smaller, and is not claimed to.

## What I did not verify

- **The timing fix has no automated test.** A latency assertion is flaky under
  CI load, so the 20.1 ms / 20.1 ms result above is a one-off manual
  measurement on one machine, five samples per branch, median reported. It is
  not protected against regression.
- **Three defects I found and deliberately left alone**, because each is a
  design gap rather than a reproduced defect, and fixing them exceeds this
  audit's scope. Each needs its own decision:
  - `src/auth/tokens.js` compares the HMAC with `!==`, a non-constant-time
    string comparison. I did not attempt to measure, let alone exploit, it; a
    remote timing attack against a base64url digest comparison across an HTTP
    stack is not practically mountable, but the constant-time fix is cheap.
  - `src/http/respond.js` rejects a body over 1 MiB only at `end`, discarding
    the excess without destroying the socket. Memory stays bounded; a client
    can still make the server read an arbitrarily large upload.
  - `POST /sessions` has no rate limit or lockout, so passwords can be
    brute-forced at whatever rate scrypt allows (~20 ms per attempt).
- **No persistence or rollout concern was assessed**, because
  `src/store/memoryStore.js` holds everything in memory. The total now comes
  from `order.total` instead of being recomputed from the items; with a real
  datastore, orders written by the old code would carry inexact totals and the
  change would need a staged migration. `toCents` would round them to the
  intended value, but that was not tested against stored data, because there is
  none.
- **No linter, type checker, or security scanner was run** — the project has
  none configured and declares no dependencies. `npm test` is the only gate.
  There is no CI workflow in the repository, so nothing enforces the new tests
  on a future change.
- **No load, concurrency, or crash-recovery testing.** The store performs
  read-modify-write without locking (`orders.markPaid` after
  `payments.capture`), which a single-threaded Node process serializes today;
  I did not analyse it for a multi-process deployment.
- **I did not run the server as documented in the README** (`npm start` with
  `APP_SECRET`/`REPORT_DIR`/`ADMIN_*`). Every probe used `createApp` over a
  real HTTP listener, which is what the test helper does.

## Files changed

```
src/app.js                |  2 +-
src/http/respond.js       | 12 +-----------
src/lib/money.js          | 18 ++++++++++++------
src/lib/pagination.js     |  2 +-
src/orders/routes.js      |  4 ++--
src/orders/service.js     |  6 +++---
src/payments/providers.js | 25 +++++++++----------------
src/payments/service.js   | 10 ++--------
src/reports/routes.js     |  4 ++++
src/users/routes.js       |  5 ++---
src/users/service.js      | 22 ++++++++++++++++-----
test/orders.test.js       | 47 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
test/reports.test.js      | 14 ++++++++++++++
```

No change to `README.md`: it described the intended behaviour correctly in every
case above, and the code now matches it.
